title: The grace before meals
hookLine: a verse said over a plate of food, where everything in the meal is Brahman
carry: brahmarpanam: giver, gift and fire are brahman
tomorrow: Arjuna asks for one answer, not two

lines: A LINE SAID OVER THE PLATE.
ONE ACT, SEEN ALL THE WAY THROUGH.
cards: Before the first bite, in some Hindu homes, someone says a line in Sanskrit over the plate. Brahmarpanam brahma havir.
It's from chapter four of the Gita, an odd thing to say before dinner: it's a verse about a fire sacrifice. The offering is Brahman. The thing offered is Brahman.
It's poured into the fire, which is Brahman, by the one offering, who is Brahman. A meal, a fire, a giver, all one.

teach.h: INACTION IN ACTION, ACTION IN INACTION.
teach.b: A few verses earlier, Krishna sets a puzzle. What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise are confused about this.

His answer: the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people, and does all their work in yoga. Shankara reads this as seeing that the Self never acts, even while the body is busy.
Ramanuja reads it as seeing knowledge of the self alive inside work done without attachment. Then Krishna describes such a person.

teach.h: ACTS BURNED IN THE FIRE OF KNOWLEDGE.
teach.b: Their acts have been burned in the fire of knowledge. They've let go of clinging to the fruit; they're always content, depending on nothing, and though they keep acting, they do nothing at all.
Then the meal verse: Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in the act goes to Brahman.

Our word has traveled since chapter three began: action you can't avoid, done as offering; action for the world, the way Janaka did it; action handed down through teachers and taken up by God; and now action seen so clearly that the doer, the deed and the fire are one thing.
Later in the chapter Krishna says it plainly: as a kindled fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ash.

teach.h: THE WEEK: FLUTE, DUST, FEARLESSNESS, WHEEL, FIRE.
teach.b: Look back over the week: Tagore's flute, God in the dust, a mind without fear.

teach.h: SEE THE ACT ALL THE WAY THROUGH.
teach.b: And the Gita's long answer to Arjuna's complaint: you can't stop acting, so learn to see what acting is.

how: Some Hindu families and schools recite Gita 4.24, 'brahmarpanam brahma havir', as a grace before meals.

o: a fire ritual only a trained priest can perform alone
action seen so clearly that doer, deed and fire are one
a meal eaten in silence, with no prayer said at all

games.q: Gita, chapter four — tap the pairs.
p: giver, gift and fire are one

s: Krishna says the question of action and inaction is easy
he says even the wise are confused about it.
the verse said before meals comes from a passage about fire sacrifice
the offering, the oblation, the fire and the one offering are all Brahman.
in chapter four, the wise person stops acting
they keep acting, but having let go of the fruit, they do nothing at all.

games.q: Krishna asks: what is action, and what is inaction? even the wise are confused. what does he say the wise one sees?
o: inaction in action, and action in inaction.
that action and inaction don't matter.
games.why: the wise one sees inaction in action and action in inaction. Shankara reads it as the Self never acting; Ramanuja as knowledge of the self alive in unattached work.

practice: Bring to mind the last thing you ate, or the next, and go through it the way the verse does: the food, the hands that lift it, the hunger it goes into, the one who's eating, each part slowly, then all of them together as one act.
If you pray, you can say the verse's opening words, brahmarpanam brahma havir, or a grace from your own tradition; if not, simply rest in the whole act at once.

wordCard.voice: Karma. In chapter four, action seen so clearly that the offering, the fire and the one who offers are one, and the act itself turns to ash in the fire of knowledge.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: brahmarpanam, the offering is Brahman. The opening word of Gita 4.24.

carryVoice: Your line: brahmarpanam: giver, gift and fire are Brahman. That's a week, and day nine hundred sixty-six.
